system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2181-11-30 05:40:00 to 2181-12-02 18:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a complex history including fibrosing mesenteritis, recurrent partial bowel obstructions, and chronic GI dysmotility, was admitted for recurrent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Imaging confirmed a partial small bowel obstruction, managed conservatively with NPO status, G-tube to gravity, IV fluids, and pain control. G-tube output decreased from over 1200 cc/day to 500–600 cc/day. She received IV iron for iron deficiency anemia and was started on TPN on hospital day 3. Abdominal massage recommended by GI helped stimulate bowel motility, leading to passage of gas and significant pain improvement. She was transitioned to a full liquid diet on day 4, tolerated it well, and was discharged on day 5. Pain management was transitioned from IV morphine to oral MS Contin and liquid morphine for breakthrough pain. She remained ambulatory throughout and was discharged home in good condition with instructions to continue full liquids and Miralax for one week.
problems: Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Recurrent small bowel obstruction, nausea and vomiting, query
SBO.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiple MDCT axial images were obtained from the base of the
lungs through the proximal thighs without intravenous contrast (secondary to
iodine allergy) but with enteric contrast.  Multiplanar reformats were
derived.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITHOUT INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  In the visualized thorax,
there is mild bibasal atelectasis.  There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  The heart is normal in size.  There is no pericardial effusion.
There is likely central venous catheter with tip at the cavoatrial junction.

In the abdomen, assessment is limited without intravenous contrast.  Within
this limitation, the liver, pancreas, spleen, and left adrenal appear normal.
There is thickening of the right adrenal gland again seen.  The kidneys are
unremarkable excepting for a small hypodensity, too small to characterize, in
the left kidney laterally, likely a simple cyst.  There is a G tube.  Small
loops of bowel are dilated and measure to 5.2 cm.  Again seen is extraluminal
hyperdense material (series 301, image 22, 24) that may represent suture
material versus sclerosing mesenteritis.  Within a central bowel loop again
seen is a tubular structure that does not appear to be connected to any
device.  This may be a GJ remnant.  There is no definite free air ro free
fluid. There is no pathologic mesenteric or retroperitoneal adenopathy.  The
abdominal aorta is normal in size and caliber.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITHOUT INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  The rectum, bladder, distal
ureters are unremarkable.  Post-hysterectomy changes are stable.  There is no
free air, free fluid or pathologic lymphadenopathy.  There is moderate fecal
loading again seen.

MUSCULOSKELETAL:  There is no suspicious osteolytic or osteoblastic lesion.
Again seen is a small bone island in the right posterior iliac.  A neural
stimulator is seen within the lower thoracic spine.

IMPRESSION:  
1. Small bowel dilation without definite transition point and with stool and
air seen in the large bowel, most consistent with an early small bowel
obstruction.  
2. Persistent tubing within the small bowel appears redundant and may be a
remnant of a GJ tube.  This may also be a focus for fibrosis and inflammation
and given that more distal loops are decompressed may play a role in the
intermittent obstructive process characteristic of this patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in this morning with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. Yesterday afternoon I tried eating a sandwich—my first solid food in a while. About two hours later, I started vomiting everything—food, liquids, even my pills. I estimated maybe 3000 cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had this before with partial bowel obstructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like my past episodes. I put my G-tube on suction right away, but not much came out. I’ve also had diarrhea—watery at first, now small pellet-like stools. No blood though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER, they did an X-ray and removed about 1500 cc from your G-tube. Your CT scan this morning shows early signs of a partial small bowel obstruction, likely triggered by advancing to solids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a full blockage? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not complete. There’s dilation in the small bowel, but air and stool are still moving into the large bowel. That’s good. We’ll manage this without surgery—NPO for now, IV fluids, and keep your G-tube on suction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not worse. But I was hoping I could finally eat solids again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your body needs time. We’ll start with clear liquids once your nausea improves. GI is consulting today to help guide the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diarrhea—should I restart Miralax?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped it for now. The diarrhea may be from the obstruction or rapid transit. We’ll monitor. Stool tests came back negative for infection, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your G-tube output has decreased from 1500 cc to about 600 cc since being NPO. That’s a good sign the bowel is calming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. My nausea is better too, especially with the Phenergan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping that on board. Your labs show mild dehydration and low hemoglobin, but stable. No signs of infection. We’ll continue IV fluids and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fibrosing mesenteritis making this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s part of the picture. The CT shows chronic changes and a possible remnant GJ tube in the bowel that could be a focus for inflammation. That may contribute to these intermittent blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that tube—it was removed years ago. I didn’t know it could still cause issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon. For now, we focus on conservative management. Tomorrow, if you’re stable, we’ll try advancing to full liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without suction on the G-tube and no vomiting. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with small sips of water, then advance to full liquids—broth, juice, pudding. We’ll watch closely for nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’m still on morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added sustained-release morphine twice daily and liquid for breakthrough pain. We’ll keep that on discharge since your pain has improved but may linger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the liquid diet well—no vomiting, good bowel sounds. GI agrees we can keep progressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you continue doing well, possibly tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re stable without G-tube suction and on a full liquid diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I take it for my DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued it at a slightly higher dose—7.5 mg daily. Your INR was in range yesterday, so that’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my dry eyes and mouth—should I keep using the drops and pilocarpine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Those help with your Sjogren’s. We’ve kept all your regular meds except adjusting timing for hospital routines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve gone over 24 hours without G-tube suction and no issues. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What should I eat when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on full liquids for the next few days—smoothies, soups, yogurt. If you’re doing well, you can slowly try soft solids, but stop if nausea or pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube? Should I keep it on suction at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you start vomiting or feel bloated. Otherwise, keep it clamped. Use it for meds if needed, but crush and dissolve them well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about warning signs? When should I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, severe pain, persistent vomiting, or blood in stool, go to the ER. Otherwise, follow up with your GI doctor in a week to discuss advancing your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds—how long should I take the morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it as prescribed for now. As your bowel function improves, you’ll likely need less. Your doctor can adjust it at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better and more confident going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you in good condition. Keep up with fluids, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Rest at home and we’ll see how you progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will go over your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready whenever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get everything set up. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take care until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep monitoring how you feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling much more hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Recovery takes time, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take it easy and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of fibrosing mesenteritis, recurrent partial small bowel obstructions, and chronic GI dysmotility, was admitted for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea after attempting to advance from liquids to solids. Imaging confirmed an early partial small bowel obstruction without a transition point, likely precipitated by dietary advancement. She was managed conservatively with NPO status, G-tube suction, IV fluids, and anti-nausea medications. G-tube output decreased significantly, and she tolerated a gradual advancement to full liquids. She remained stable without suction for over 24 hours prior to discharge. Stool studies were negative for infection. She was discharged home in good condition on a full liquid diet with instructions to avoid solids for several days and follow up with GI. Pain was managed with oral morphine, and all home medications were continued with minor adjustments.
